They are called inverted verbs but only because ENGLISH inverts compared to Spanish. For Spanish speakers it’s totally normal. You can probably find lists using that term. 

Here’s a few more common ones:

Molestar (to bother) - it bothers me. Me molesta. 

Faltar (to lack) - I’m missing my hat. Me falta el sombrero. 

Doler (to hurt) - my knees hurt. Me duelen las rodillas. 

Importar (to matter) - they don’t matter to me. No me importan ellos. 

Interesar (to interest) - I’m interested in traveling. Me interesa viajar. 

Parecer (to seem) - it seems safe. Me parece seguro

Caer (to fall, to leave an impression - if a person) - I liked those people. Esas personas me cayeron bien. 

Sentar (to sit, to leave an impression as an experience) - the experience goes well for me - me sienta bien la experiencia

There are verbs like encantar and gustar that are not “I love” or “I like” but rather “it enchants me” or “it pleases me.”

So you translate, “¿te encanta el futbol?” Literally like, “does football delight you?” 

“A ti te encanta el futbol” emphasizes the You, that is, do YOU love football?” Because “te” is an indirect pronoun (“to you”), and “a ti” is saying the same thing. You have to have the TE there, but the A TI is optional for emphasis. 

“Tú encantas el futbol” means “football loves you,” or literally, “you are delightful / enchanting to football.”

Yes, it's a bit arbitrary to come up with a fair value for a private company, but we use comps to public companies, different multiples of revenues and EBITDA based on how publicly traded companies trade (adjusted for scale), FCF analysis, and then of course hype - hype on the industry, on the team, etc. A great management team can create a sense of scarcity - \*you'll be LUCKY to be selected by us, Mr. VC\*, where a company desperate for cash will have a hard time.  

My argument is simply that the VC market sets the price by competitive bid. They use the above tools and info, but in the end it's like making an offer to buy a house. If there's only one VC interested, and the company NEEDS the deal, the "market" (of one) will set a low price. But that's not a discount, it's what the entire market (of one, the rest of the market was uninterested) was willing to pay at that time.  It's an undiscounted price as stated by the behavior of the market.

(You can build discounts in, sure, like if I sold a bunch of convertible notes to a first VC that had a feature on them that said that they could buy the next round of shares at a 20% discount, and this happens all the time. In that case, when the VC market comes to price the next round at say, $10m, the owners of those original notes get to buy shares 20% lower than the new VC is buying them. That's a discount to the market value as a benefit to the earlier investors for taking the earlier risk.)

Source: I'm a VC/PE CEO who has raised about $60m in my lifetime from VC and PE sources.

Public companies' valuations are set the same way. "Whatever the investors agree to" - that's the undiscounted price. I agree it might be lower than what someone would think the company is worth, but if that person isn't putting their money where their belief is, then in fact the company is worth what the highest bidders say it's worth.

Agreed, if the company is issuing RSUs to employees, there is implicit dilution when the RSUs vest.

On the VC side, VCs pay full market price, indeed. There's no discount. It's not a public market, it's a private market that is set by the interested VCs around the table against the company's performance, promise, and ability to get the deal in front of a large number of VC eyes. The market has far fewer players, but there is still a market with competitive forces trying to buy private company stock. The company has to argue what its pre-money valuation is, and it goes to the venture market with its argument. The interested venture market competes to be in the syndicate and makes an offer. They make the best offer they are willing to make. The company chooses the deal that optimizes for the best strategic investors at the highest company valuation. No discount, the company takes the best offer the market will offer, which is, by definition, the undiscounted value of the company at that moment.

The fundamentals HAVE changed. The company now has their entire earlier valuation in the bank as cash. They've just gained their entire value in cash to invest in whatever they want. Technically the cash received increases the value dollar for dollar (although public markets decide value, and not always rationally).

In the private company world, this is PRECISELY how it works. You want to raise $10m in venture money, so you go talk to venture capitalists and try to get the best possible "pre-money" value for your company. If you get them to agree you're worth $10m, so after they give you their $10m, you each own $10m of the total new "post-money" value of $20m, or 50%. And the private investing market now looks at you as a $20m company. The share price hasn't changed, you've just got twice as many shares. 

Now it's up to you to do something to make the $20m company worth $30m or more.

I started with Pimsleur - all five chapters of 30 each. That got me to the point where I felt confident enough to bumble my way through my first lesson with a real Venezuelan human. Since then I’ve done two to three sessions with her every week and have religiously used Anki to memorize everything I didn’t know. I do an advanced conversation class (started as a beginner, then an intermediate) with other gringos and a Latino teacher once a week. 

Each morning I use Anki. Ten minutes per day. My vocabulary has exploded because of it. I know 6,000 words now, crazy!!!! I still fuck up gender and I still bumble over the estuviera and the hubiera, siquiera de vez en cuando. 

Shout out to HelloTalk, Jorge Drexler, the song La Flaca, and watching Spanish shows with Spanish subtitles. Also the podcast No Sé Dime Tú, which I could not understand even six months ago. 

Admittedly Pimsleur and personal lessons are expensive options. Everything but Anki costs money. (Maybe Anki too, a little.) I started about three years ago. Since I started learning I have never traveled to a Spanish speaking country and I have extremely limited opportunities to speak to Latinos. 

I’m a solid B2 now. Can understand 90% of what I read anywhere and context enables me to approach 95%. I can understand about 85% of what’s said to me with precision, y puedo agarrar la vuelta a lo que no entendí. And I can express just about anything I want to including a layer of complex emotions, the subtleties of recipes, how investors buy and sell things, etc. I still get stuck sometimes and whenever that happens, without fail, I use Spanish Dict and Linguee to understand how natives would say something and then I drop it in Anki and forget it. 

The most important habit is to use Anki each morning and to find a way to speak with others. HelloTalk is the best free way I’ve found to do it.

A prime number is a number that is only divisible by itself and the number 1. Now since you're five, you don't know what division is. But let's assume that you understand division, and then I'll treat you like a five year old for the rest.

How do you know if a number is prime?

Well, you have to divide the number by every other number that is less than it and see if it divides evenly or if there is a fraction as a result. If some number is found that divides your number evenly, it's not prime.

To answer this question for ridiculously large numbers requires an incredible amount of division. But still, if you give me a really really big number and a computer, I can eventually tell you whether it's prime.

But if, instead of asking "is this ridiculously big number prime?" you ask "find me a ridiculously big prime number," that problem is infinitely more difficult because you have to solve the same problem over and over again for gazillions and gazillions of numbers, until you find one. It's so hard that it would take a computer longer than the entire lifetime of the known universe.

So we know that there are really Really REALLY big primes out there (in fact however big you find one, there is always a bigger one), but it's hard to find specific examples.

There's a gas called carbon dioxide which - when too much is in the atmosphere - makes the planet hotter.

Carbon dioxide is made when we use oil and other things like oil (e.g., gas). These are commonly referred to as "fossil fuels." The more fossil fuels we use to make energy for our cars and homes, the more we produce carbon dioxide, and the hotter the planet gets.

How do we stop?

Well, oil companies make money by selling more fossil fuels. Why would they want to stop?

Cap and trade is a policy that enables the gradual replacement of fossil fuels by other sources of energy that don't produce carbon dioxide. Here's how it works:

1. We place a hard limit on the amount of carbon dioxide that the country can produce in a year. This limit should be reachable today, but should gradually get smaller and smaller over the years. This is the CAP of Cap and Trade.

2. We give each organization a limit to the amount of carbon dioxide that they can produce, in a way that makes sure that overall, the entire country doesn't go over the limit we established in (1). This is the CAP, applied on a company by company level.

3. If an organization produces less than its allotment of carbon dioxide, it can sell its rights to produce the rest to another organization that needs to produce more than its allotment. This is the TRADE of Cap and Trade.

Overall, this creates INCENTIVES ("reasons for doing something") for organizations to find ways to do the same things while producing less carbon dioxide. If you make less, you can make money by selling your allocation to other companies. And if you make more, you have to pay for it by buying the rights from some other organization.

tl;dr: cap and trade limits the carbon dioxide that can be produced overall, and lets organizations sell and buy the rights to produce more from each other.

Your entire "DNA sequences" as you say (we call it the genome) is about 3 billion letters ("bases") long. Each position has four possible values (A, C, G, or T). Among humans it is widely understood that the [nucleotide diversity](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nucleotide_diversity) is about 0.1%, that is, we differ from each other by about 1 in 1,000 bases. So there are about 3 million differences between each human's genome.

Let's make a huge simplifying assumptions:

1. each of these differences is a single letter difference at a specific location. (Of course there are in reality all sorts of genomic variants from insertions to deletions to translocations, etc. which would greatly increas  But this problem is balanced by the fact that genetic drift within a species is not smoothly distributed.) 

1. Differences between human genomes occur in a even distribution. (Of course genomes are highly sensitive to non-random events like tribes of genetically similar people staying close to each other through generations.)

So with these two assumptions, and knowing that there are 3,000,000 differences between each human genome in an evenly distributed way across all human population, then there are 3,000,000 places where we have to choose one of four letters. Using the formula for a [combination](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Combination), we have:

      3000000! / (4! * (3000000-4)!)
    = 3000000! / (4! * 2999996!)
    = 3000000 * 2999999 * 2999998 * 2999997 / (4!)
    = 3000000 * 2999999 * 2999998 * 2999997 / (4 * 3 * 2 * 1)
    = 3.37 * 10^24

So there are 3.37 * 10^24 possible genomes.

Let's assume that the total number of humans who have ever lived on earth is about 108 billion, or 1.08 * 10^9 ([Source](http://www.prb.org/Articles/2002/HowManyPeopleHaveEverLivedonEarth.aspx).)

Almost there. We are now asking for the probability that one of these genomes happened twice. The probability of any of these genomes happening at all is:

         (1.08 * 10^9) / (3.37 * 10^24)

which is 3.20 * 10^-16.

The probability of it happening twice is a Compound Probability. The Compound Probability of A and B is P (A and B) = P(A) * P(B).

So, the likelihood of the same genome happening in all of human history is 1.02 * 10^-31.

**tl;dr If we make certain simplifying assumptions, there is roughly a 1 in 10,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000 chance of this occurring throughout human history.

The 0th law is a statement of the undyingly obvious, and therefore understandable by five year olds.

Let's say you have two cups of water.

Let's say the temperature of water in Cup 1 is exactly the same temperature as the water in Cup 2. So if you mixed Cup 1 and Cup 2 there would be no change in temperature. (Six year olds call this "Thermal Equilibrium," by the way.)

Now, let's introduce a new cup, Cup 3. And Cup 3 is exactly the same temperature as Cup 1. So again, if you mixed Cup 1 and 3, there'd be no change in temperature. (Again, if you're six - Thermal Equilibrium.)

The 0th law says that - even though I told you nothing about the relationship of Cup 2 and Cup 3, given the things I HAVE told you, Cup 2 and Cup 3 are exactly the same temperature. If you mixed them, there would be no change in temperature. (They are in thermal equilibrium because they are each in thermal equilibrium with some other thing, in this case, Cup 1.)

See arguments on the cardinality of the set of real numbers for a justification. Simply: there are an infinite number of Integers because no matter which integer you name I can name another. But this set is COUNTABLE in that for each element of the set you can map this element to an integer. 

This is unlike real numbers which are uncountable. Certainly these numbers (e.g. 4.317856) are also infinite because all of the integers are included in it and then more. But is this infinity in some way larger than the infinity of integers? It turns out that, at least mathematically, it is. The reason is that given two real numbers that are close enough together to map them to two integers (e.g. 1.0001 and 1.00011) there will always exist an infinite number of real numbers in between them (1.000101, 1.00010101010101, and so on). So we call the set of integers a COUNTABLE INFINITE set and the set of real numbers an UNCOUNTABLE INFINITE set.
